::: {.callout-tip title="What you will be able to do"}
- Compress any sparse set of values into dense ranks and say precisely which information the translation keeps (order and equality) and which it destroys (gaps, sums, residues, gcds) (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-srt-a4).
- Implement a Fenwick tree over compressed ranks — point add, prefix sum, and `kth` descent — and use it for "how many earlier values are smaller?" questions in $O(n \log n)$ (@sec-coord-a2).
- Recognise when a batch of queries can be reordered (offline) and when updates interleaved with queries forbid it (online), and answer offline queries in the order that suits the data, then restore the input order (@sec-coord-a3).
- Turn "for each threshold $t$, an aggregate over all elements $\le t$" into one sorted pass plus a prefix table, priced at $O(n \log n + q \log n)$ or $O(n \log n + q)$ (@sec-coord-a4, @sec-coord-p2-lequal).
- Convert a stream of deletions into a stream of insertions by running time backwards, and combine it with an incremental structure (last-occurrence, DSU-style block merging) to answer "state after each deletion" (@sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3-destroy).
- Sweep a sorted list of $+1/-1$ events over coordinates up to $10^{18}$ and report how many integer points have each coverage count, using the $r+1$ convention to make closed intervals exact (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered).
- Compress two dimensions — both axes of a rectangle union, or the whole $n(n-1)/2$ pair universe of a graph down to the $\le 2k$ vertices that can matter (@sec-coord-p5-area, @sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
:::

## Why this matters {#sec-coord-why}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Two sentences appear in problem statements over and over. *"The values can be up to $10^9$"* and *"answer the queries in the order given."* The first is a memory problem: a table indexed by value would need a billion cells. The second is a scheduling problem: you would rather answer queries in a smarter order than the one they arrive in. **Coordinate compression** kills the first — replace each value by its position in the sorted list of *distinct* values, so a billion-wide universe becomes $n$-wide. **Offline processing** kills the second — sort the queries by whatever key makes the data move in one direction, answer them on a single pass, and print the answers in the original order. Both ideas are just sorting wearing different hats, and together they unlock the whole "large values, many queries" corner of competitive programming.
:::

Chapter @sec-srt introduced the rank map as a one-liner (@sec-srt-a4) and Chapter @sec-mex showed what a *small value domain* buys you (a table indexed by value, @sec-mex-a6). This chapter is the marriage of the two: when the value domain is huge, *manufacture* a small one. The rank table is exactly the object @sec-cnt-a3, @sec-salgo-p2 and several @sec-mex lessons kept promising — "a Fenwick tree over compressed values, a later chapter's tool". Here is that tool, and here are the four habits that surround it: sort the queries, run time backwards, sweep the coordinate line, and compress both dimensions.

Three constraint shapes tell you you are in this chapter's territory:

| Statement hint | What it forbids / enables | Which section uses it |
|---|---|---|
| $1 \le a_i \le 10^9$ but $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$, and only *comparisons* matter | No table indexed by raw value; ranks are dense | @sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-p1 |
| "Answer $q$ queries" with **no updates interleaved** | Queries may be reordered — sort them | @sec-coord-a3, @sec-coord-a4 |
| "After each deletion / removal / undo, report …" | Insertions are easy, deletions are not: go backwards | @sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3 |
| Segment endpoints up to $10^{18}$; "how many points covered by exactly $k$" | Per-point loops impossible; per-*event* loops fine | @sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4 |

The whole chapter in one pipe: a huge or messy coordinate universe is translated, once in $O(n \log n)$, into dense indices — and every table, sweep pointer, and Fenwick cell downstream is sized by $n$, never by the values.

The lessons build the toolkit in six steps:

- **A1 — The rank map.** What the translation preserves, what it destroys, and the three ways to write it (@sec-coord-a1).
- **A2 — A Fenwick tree over ranks.** Point add, prefix sum, and `kth` descent in a dozen lines (@sec-coord-a2).
- **A3 — Offline versus online.** When reordering queries is legal, and the sort-by-index / restore-by-index idiom (@sec-coord-a3).
- **A4 — Sorting queries by threshold.** One sorted pass plus a prefix table answers a whole batch (@sec-coord-a4).
- **A5 — Reverse processing.** Turn deletions into insertions and replay time backwards (@sec-coord-a5).
- **A6 — Sweeps and two-dimensional ranks.** $+1/-1$ events over $10^{18}$ coordinates; compress both axes (@sec-coord-a6).

Part B turns the toolkit into five patterns, one per outline topic: compress-then-index (@sec-coord-p1), sort the queries and scan once (@sec-coord-p2), reverse the stream of operations (@sec-coord-p3), sweep the line and answer (@sec-coord-p4), and compress the space you actually touch (@sec-coord-p5).

## Part A — Lessons

## A1. The rank map: translation, not arithmetic {#sec-coord-a1}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A rank map is a translation from values to their positions in the sorted distinct list. Translation preserves *comparisons*: if $x < y$ before, then $\mathit{rank}(x) < \mathit{rank}(y)$ after; equal values get equal ranks. Translation does **not** preserve *arithmetic*: the gap between $10^6$ and $3$ becomes the gap between $3$ and $1$. Use the map whenever the problem only ever asks "smaller? equal? between?" — and stay in the original values whenever it adds, subtracts, takes mod, or gcds.
:::

The one-line recipe is from @sec-srt-a4; the three variants and their costs are worth having in muscle memory before the problems need them.

```{python}
def rank_map(vals):
    """value -> dense 1-based rank; equal values share a rank (the @sec-srt-a4 one-liner)."""
    return {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(vals)))}


r = rank_map([40, 10, 20, 30, 10, -5])
assert r[-5] == 1 and r[10] == 2 and r[20] == 3 and r[30] == 4 and r[40] == 5
assert len(r) == 5     # five distinct values, ranks 1..5 — a table of n+1 cells fits

# The dict-free variant: sort the distinct values once, bisect per lookup.
sd = sorted(set([40, 10, 20, 30, 10, -5]))
assert [bisect.bisect_left(sd, v) + 1 for v in (40, 10, 20, 30, -5)] == [5, 2, 3, 4, 1]

for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 15))]
    m, sd = rank_map(arr), sorted(set(arr))
    assert all(m[x] == bisect.bisect_left(sd, x) + 1 for x in arr)
    # the contract from @sec-srt-a4: order-reflecting and equality-preserving
    for x in arr:
        for y in arr:
            assert (m[x] < m[y]) == (x < y) and (m[x] == m[y]) == (x == y)
```

The two variants differ in what they cost and what they allow. The **dict** gives $O(1)$ lookups and *stable ranks* (the map survives as long as the value set is fixed); it needs $O(n)$ memory and hashing. **Bisect on the sorted list** needs no hash map — the C++ `lower_bound` twin is the standard move when the hash is attackable (@sec-lang-p7) — and costs an $O(\log n)$ search per lookup, but it also answers the *reverse* question, "what value has rank $j$", by indexing the sorted list. When queries **insert new values** as they arrive, neither survives unchanged: the dict must be rebuilt or replaced by a structure that tolerates a growing universe (that is a balanced-tree / order-statistics topic the trees volume takes up; a pragmatic contest trick is to *read all queries first* and compress over every value that will ever appear — the offline permission again).

What translation destroys — with a witness:

```{python}
vals = [3, 5, 10**6]
m = rank_map(vals)
assert (m[3], m[5], m[10**6]) == (1, 2, 3)
assert (10**6 - 3) != m[10**6] - m[3]          # gaps are gone
assert (10**6 % 7) != (m[10**6] % 7)           # residues are gone
```

So CF 1294D's residue buckets (@sec-mex-p2-mex-max) and every @sec-gcd-a1 multiple-walk must run on *raw* values: they ask arithmetic questions. The problems in Part B ask only ordering questions — "smaller", "between", "first missing" — which is exactly the certificate that compression is legal. One more distinction to keep straight:

::: {#fig-coord-rankmap}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
rm_a = [40, 10, 20, 30, 10, 50]
rm_m = rank_map(rm_a)
assert rm_m[50] == 5 and rm_m[10] == 1
rm_keys = ("values", "sorted(set)", "rank[x]")
rm_cells = [
    [str(x) for x in rm_a],
    [str(x) for x in sorted(set(rm_a))] + [""],
    [str(rm_m[x]) for x in rm_a],
]


def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, rm_cells, row_labels=list(rm_keys),
           colors={(ri, ci): c for ri, c in ((0, "muted"), (2, "indigo")) for ci in range(6)},
           cell_w=1.25)
V.show(draw)
```

The middle row is the only thing stored besides the dict: rank $= 1 +$ position there. Duplicate `10`s share rank 1; five distinct values earn a five-wide table — the $10^9$-wide original range never allocates anything.

:::

- **Compress values** when a table/structure is indexed by value (@sec-coord-p1).
- **Compress positions** when the *indices* are huge but only $O(n)$ of them exist — CF 540E's sequence positions reach $10^9$ (@sec-coord-p1-invinfinite), and CF 1000C's segment endpoints reach $10^{18}$ (@sec-coord-p4-covered). The rank map is the same; point the arrow at the other array.
- **Compress both** when a 2D universe collapses to a $2n$-cell grid (LC 850, @sec-coord-p5-area).

## A2. A Fenwick tree over ranks {#sec-coord-a2}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A prefix-sum table answers "how many / how much among the first $j$" in $O(1)$ — as long as nothing changes. The moment you must *remove* a value from the table (or add one), a plain prefix table costs $O(n)$ per edit. A **Fenwick tree** (binary indexed tree) keeps the same question answerable in $O(\log n)$ per edit *and* per read, by storing each partial sum at the index whose binary form ends in the run of zeros covering exactly that range. It is the structure every earlier chapter kept pointing at — "@sec-cnt-a3 promises a Fenwick tree over compressed values" — and compressed ranks are precisely the indices it wants.
:::

Ten lines, three operations; the full derivation of why the `i & -i` walk works belongs to the trees volume (ch. 175 of the roadmap), but nothing in this chapter needs more than the three behaviours below.

```{python}
class BIT:
    """Fenwick tree over indices 1..n: point add, prefix sum, and kth-by-prefix descent."""

    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (n + 1)

    def add(self, i, delta):
        while i <= self.n:
            self.t[i] += delta
            i += i & -i                 # i & -i = lowest set bit

    def sum(self, i):
        """sum over 1..i;  when i == 0 the empty sum."""
        s = 0
        while i > 0:
            s += self.t[i]
            i -= i & -i
        return s

    def range_sum(self, l, r):
        return self.sum(r) - self.sum(l - 1)

    def kth(self, k):
        """smallest index i with sum(i) >= k;  entries non-negative, 1 <= k <= sum(n)."""
        i, step = 0, 1 << (self.n.bit_length() - 1)
        while step:
            j = i + step
            if j <= self.n and self.t[j] < k:
                i, k = j, k - self.t[j]
            step //= 2
        return i + 1


b = BIT(8)
for idx, d in [(3, 5), (5, 2), (8, 1)]:
    b.add(idx, d)
assert b.sum(2) == 0 and b.sum(3) == 5 and b.sum(5) == 7 and b.range_sum(4, 5) == 2
assert b.kth(1) == 3 and b.kth(6) == 5 and b.kth(8) == 8

for _ in range(200):
    n = random.randint(1, 40)
    naive = [0] * n
    b = BIT(n)
    for _ in range(60):
        i = random.randint(1, n)
        d = random.randint(0, 9)        # non-negative keeps kth() meaningful
        naive[i - 1] += d
        b.add(i, d)
    assert b.sum(n) == sum(naive)
    total = sum(naive)
    if total:
        k = random.randint(1, total)
        acc = 0
        for idx, v in enumerate(naive, 1):
            acc += v
            if acc >= k:
                assert b.kth(k) == idx
                break
```

::: {#fig-coord-bit}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
bit_a = [0, 0, 5, 0, 2, 0, 0, 1]
bit_t = [0] * 9
bit_n = 8
idx_, d = 3, 5
while idx_ <= bit_n:
    bit_t[idx_] += d
    idx_ += idx_ & -idx_
idx_ = 5
while idx_ <= bit_n:
    bit_t[idx_] += 2
    idx_ += idx_ & -idx_
idx_ = 8
while idx_ <= bit_n:
    bit_t[idx_] += 1
    idx_ += idx_ & -idx_
COVERAGE = {1: "1", 2: "1-2", 3: "3", 4: "1-4", 5: "5", 6: "5-6", 7: "7", 8: "1-8"}


def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [
        [str(x) for x in bit_a[1:]],
        [str(x) for x in bit_t[1:]],
        [COVERAGE[i] for i in range(1, 9)],
    ], row_labels=["a[1..8]", "t[1..8]", "t[i] covers"], colors={(1, i): "indigo" for i in range(8)},
        cell_w=0.95)
V.show(draw)
```

Each `t[i]` stores the sum over the range $(i - \mathit{lowbit}(i), i]$; `add(3, 5)` updates $t[3], t[4], t[8]$ — exactly the cells whose ranges contain index $3$. Prefix reads walk *down* by removing lowbits: `sum(7) = t[7] + t[6] + t[4]`.

:::

Three habits make the BIT pay off in this chapter. **(1) Prefix sums over *ranks* answer "how many seen values are $\le v$?"** — one `add(rank(v), 1)` per seen value and one `sum` per question. **(2) A *second* BIT for a weighted sum** (the classic "count *and* total of earlier smaller values") turns counts into sums with no new ideas — seen in @sec-coord-p4-moving. **(3) `kth` descent finds the first prefix reaching a target** — "remove this value, give me the $j$-th survivor" (@sec-coord-p3-restore), and "the first rank whose cell is free" is the MEX-of-a-changing-set the @sec-mex-pit exercise pointed at. `kth` costs $O(\log n)$ because the descent is a binary search written directly on the tree's own partial sums.

```{python}
# The "how many earlier values are smaller" pattern in three lines, on ranks.
def earlier_smaller_counts(a):
    m = rank_map(a)
    n = len(m)
    bt, out = BIT(n), []
    for x in a:
        rx = m[x]
        out.append(bt.sum(rx - 1))      # strictly smaller = prefix below this rank
        bt.add(rx, 1)
    return out


assert earlier_smaller_counts([5, 3, 4, 1, 2]) == [0, 0, 1, 0, 1]
for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(-30, 30) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    assert earlier_smaller_counts(arr) == [
        sum(1 for y in arr[:i] if y < x) for i, x in enumerate(arr)
    ]
```

The `for y in arr[:i]` oracle is the same quadratic witness the merge-sort count of @sec-salgo-p2 is stress-tested against; the BIT version is $O(n \log n)$ and — unlike merge sort — also survives *interleaved* questions (which is why the trees volume prefers it).

## A3. Offline versus online: what reordering may cost you {#sec-coord-a3}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A query problem is **online** when the next question may depend on the previous answer, or when updates and questions are interleaved — then you must answer in arrival order, with a structure ready at every step. It is **offline** when the input array is fixed for the whole batch: you already *know* every query, so you may answer them in whatever order makes the data move monotonically, storing each answer under its original index for later printing.
:::

The permission is stated most cheaply in @sec-pref's difference-array clause: "many updates, **then** one reading" is $O(1)$ per update; interleave a single query and the reading cost returns. Offline permission is the same lever pulled harder: not just *delaying* reads but *reordering* them. The idiom is two lines — sort the query **indices**, answer into a separate array — and the discipline is never to print while you sweep.

```{python}
def offline_le_count(a, queries):
    """for each threshold q count elements of a <= q, answering queries in sorted order."""
    sa = sorted(a)
    order = sorted(range(len(queries)), key=lambda i: queries[i])   # sort INDICES, not pairs
    ans = [0] * len(queries)
    j = 0
    for qi in order:
        while j < len(sa) and sa[j] <= queries[qi]:
            j += 1                        # the pointer only ever moves right
        ans[qi] = j                       # restored to input order here, not printed here
    return ans


assert offline_le_count([2, 1, 4, 3], [2, 5, 0]) == [2, 4, 0]
for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(-20, 20) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    qs = [random.randint(-25, 25) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 8))]
    assert offline_le_count(arr, qs) == [sum(1 for x in arr if x <= q) for q in qs]
```

Compare the cost ledger against the naive per-query scan: both read the array once, but the offline version paid one sort and then moved the pointer a *total* of $n$ steps across all $q$ queries — $O(n \log n + n + q)$ versus $O(nq)$. The binary-search form (`sum(x <= q)` via `bisect_right` per query, $O(n \log n + q \log n)$) is the *same sweep* with the pointer replaced by `bisect`, and it does **not** need query reordering: when a statement secretly forbids reordering (updates interleaved — "modify $a_i$, then ask", or interactive input), `bisect` on a *static* sorted copy is your only option, and anything with updates pushes you to the BIT/segment-tree side of the ledger (the online form of @sec-coord-p4-moving's count+sum pair).

Two failure modes to keep in mind, both cheap to avoid:

- **Reordering when answers feed later queries.** "Given the answer to query $i$, choose query $i+1$" is not a batch — the sweep has a moving target. Offline is only for *independent* questions about a *fixed* object.
- **Losing the index.** A common contest bug is answering in sorted order and printing in sorted order. `ans[qi] = value` is the whole discipline: an answer *array*, written at the original index, printed after the sweep.

## A4. Sorting the queries by threshold {#sec-coord-a4}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A *threshold query* asks about everything on one side of a moving cut: "elements $\le t$", "edges of weight $\le w$", "points covered while the window reaches $t$". Sort the data once, sort the queries once, and let a single pointer walk the data as the threshold rises. Each element is consumed exactly once across the whole batch — $q$ queries, $n + q$ steps. When the aggregate itself must be *read* at arbitrary moments instead of swept monotonically, the same sorted array answers any threshold in $O(\log n)$ with `bisect` over a prefix table.
:::

The one sorted pass that answers every threshold has a companion trick worth isolating: make the pass *reusable* by caching what the prefix contains at every cut — a prefix-sum table over the sorted data.

```{python}
def threshold_table(a):
    """sort once; then count AND sum of elements <= t are two O(log n) reads forever."""
    sa = sorted(a)
    pre = [0]
    for x in sa:
        pre.append(pre[-1] + x)
    return sa, pre


def query_le(sa, pre, t):
    j = bisect.bisect_right(sa, t)
    return j, pre[j]


sa, pre = threshold_table([4, -1, 3, 3, 9])
assert query_le(sa, pre, 3) == (3, 5) and query_le(sa, pre, -2) == (0, 0)
assert query_le(sa, pre, 9) == (5, 18)
for _ in range(200):
    arr = [random.randint(-15, 15) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 12))]
    sa, pre = threshold_table(arr)
    t = random.randint(-20, 20)
    j, s = query_le(sa, pre, t)
    assert j == sum(1 for x in arr if x <= t)
    assert s == sum(x for x in arr if x <= t)
```

That pair — a `(count, sum)` read at any threshold — is exactly the shape of two Part B problems' inner loop: @sec-coord-p2-lequal asks only the count; @sec-coord-p4-moving asks count *and* sum of coordinates among velocities $\le v$, with the velocities compressed (@sec-coord-a2's two-BIT habit replaces the prefix table when the swept order is not the sorted order).

The pointer form (A3's sweep) and the table form above are interchangeable for pure thresholds. The table form stays *online* — any query arrives, answered in $O(\log n)$, no reordering needed — at the price that the underlying data must still be static. When queries reorder **and** the data is a tree/graph (edges entering the pool as $w$ grows), the monotone pointer becomes a monotone **structure**: DSU merges as the threshold rises — @sec-coord-p2-pathq.

## A5. Reverse processing: undo by replaying backwards {#sec-coord-a5}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
Deletion is hard for incremental structures: removing a number from the middle of "the largest block sum", or an edge from the middle of a connectivity answer, generally needs the whole thing rebuilt. Insertion is easy: blocks merge, components grow, sums accumulate. If a problem hands you a sequence of **deletions** and asks a question after each one, run the sequence **backwards**: you start from the empty final state and *insert* in reverse. The $k$-th backward insertion lands you exactly in the state "after $k$ deletions" of the forward time.
:::

Reverse replay is the same permission as A3 in disguise — you may answer *later* what you were asked *earlier*, because answers are stored, not printed — but it adds a second dimension: *direction of time*. Here is the skeleton, exercised on the archetypal statement (CF 722C, solved end-to-end with a contest write-up at @sec-coord-p3-destroy):

```{python}
def max_block_after_deletions(a, order):
    """1-based deletion order; return the max contiguous-block sum after each deletion."""
    n = len(a)
    live = [False] * n
    parent, tot = list(range(n)), [0] * n

    def find(x):
        while parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
            x = parent[x]
        return x

    def merge(x, y):
        rx, ry = find(x), find(y)
        if rx != ry:
            parent[ry] = rx
            tot[rx] += tot[ry]
        return tot[find(rx)]

    ans = [0] * (n + 1)              # ans[k] = best after the first k deletions
    best = 0
    for k in range(n - 1, -1, -1):   # replay time backwards: re-add deletion step k+1
        x = order[k] - 1
        live[x] = True
        parent[x] = x
        tot[x] = a[x]
        best = max(best, tot[x])
        for y in (x - 1, x + 1):
            if 0 <= y < n and live[y]:
                best = max(best, merge(x, y))
        ans[k] = best                # state == "first k deletions applied"
    return ans[1:]                   # after each of deletions 1..n; ans[n] = empty = 0


def max_block_brute(a, order):
    out = []
    arr = list(a)
    for p in order:
        arr[p - 1] = None
        best = cur = 0
        for x in arr:
            if x is None:
                cur = 0
            else:
                cur += x
                best = max(best, cur)
        out.append(best)
    return out


assert max_block_after_deletions([1, 5, 2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1, 2, 5]) == \
       max_block_brute([1, 5, 2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1, 2, 5])
for _ in range(300):
    arr = [random.randint(0, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 10))]
    od = list(range(1, len(arr) + 1))
    random.shuffle(od)
    assert max_block_after_deletions(arr, od) == max_block_brute(arr, od)
```

::: {#fig-coord-reverse}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
rv_a, rv_od = [1, 5, 2, 3, 1], [3, 4, 1, 2, 5]
rv_fwd = max_block_after_deletions(rv_a, rv_od)
rv_rows = []
rv_state = list(rv_a)
for step, (p, bs) in enumerate(zip(rv_od, rv_fwd), 1):
    rv_state[p - 1] = None
    rv_rows.append(dict(values=[str(x) if x is not None else "x" for x in rv_state],
                        label=f"delete pos {p}  ->  best {bs}"))
rv_state = [None] * len(rv_a)
for step, p in enumerate(reversed(rv_od), 1):
    rv_state[p - 1] = rv_a[p - 1]
    rv_rows.append(dict(values=[str(x) if x is not None else "." for x in rv_state],
                        label=f"reverse step {step}: re-add {p}"))


def draw(ax, p):
    V.trace(ax, p, rv_rows[:3] + rv_rows[-2:], gap=3.3)
V.show(draw)
```

Top three rows: forward deletions with the question after each. Bottom two rows: the same timeline played backwards — each row is the state of a forward *answer point*; "x" deleted, "." not yet re-added.

:::

Reverse replay also repairs Python's missing-deletion problem (@sec-lang-p4): a `set` loses arbitrary elements gracefully, but the "largest available $\le x$" family (Concert Tickets, @sec-lang-p4-tickets) *is* an undo problem in disguise — process customers largest-ticket-first and the DSU only *marks* positions gone. The pattern list for this chapter: whenever the hard direction of your operation has a lazy, monotone, easy inverse ("add" vs "delete", "merge" vs "split", "activate" vs "erase"), flip the timeline.

## A6. Sweeps and the two-dimensional rank map {#sec-coord-a6}

::: {.callout-note title="In plain words"}
A sweep is A4's pointer given a geometric job. Sort all *interesting coordinates* (segment endpoints, event times), then move a cut through them, maintaining a small running state (count active, total active weight, …). Between two consecutive interesting coordinates nothing changes — so the sweep charges you per *event*, never per *unit of space*: a $10^{18}$-long line with $4 \cdot 10^5$ endpoints is one $O(n \log n)$ sort and one $O(n)$ walk. The 2D version: compress **each axis independently**; the rectangles' sides define a grid of at most $2n \times 2n$ cells inside which coverage is constant, and every cell is one rectangle test.
:::

The event-sweep foundation is in @sec-int-events / @sec-int-p2 ("turn intervals into $+1/-1$ points"); the upgrade here is *counting integer points per coverage level* over a $10^{18}$ universe with the $r+1$ convention from @sec-int-repr:

```{python}
def coverage_counts(segs):
    """closed integer segments [(l, r)]; return Counter: k = number of segments exactly k covers."""
    events = []
    for l, r in segs:
        events.append((l, 1))
        events.append((r + 1, -1))       # r+1: points p in [l, r] live in [l, r+1)
    events.sort()
    cnt, cur, prev, i = Counter(), 0, events[0][0], 0
    while i < len(events):
        x = events[i][0]
        if x > prev:
            cnt[cur] += x - prev         # the run prev..x-1 all has coverage cur
            prev = x
        while i < len(events) and events[i][0] == x:
            cur += events[i][1]          # apply ALL deltas at this coordinate, then move on
            i += 1
    return cnt


c = coverage_counts([(0, 3), (1, 2), (2, 5)])
assert c[1] == 3 and c[2] == 2 and c[3] == 1     # 0,3,4 once; 1,2 twice; 2 thrice — 2 counted in both
for _ in range(200):
    segs = [(min(l, r), max(l, r))
            for l, r in ((random.randint(0, 14), random.randint(0, 14))
                         for _ in range(random.randint(1, 5)))]
    naive_total = 0
    exact = Counter()
    for p in range(0, 15):
        exact[sum(1 for l, r in segs if l <= p <= r)] += 1
    got = coverage_counts(segs)
    assert {k: v for k, v in got.items() if k} == {k: v for k, v in exact.items() if k}
```

The inner loop detail that hides bugs is the **grouping**: several events can share a coordinate (one segment ends where another starts; two degenerate points collide); you must apply all deltas at $x$ *after* charging the stretch $\mathit{prev} \to x{-}1$ with the *old* count. The 2D preview that Part B's last pattern cashes:

```{python}
# 2D compression: unique sorted x-coords and y-coords define cells whose interior is uniform.
rects = [(0, 0, 3, 2), (2, 1, 5, 4)]           # (x1, y1, x2, y2), half-open on the far edges
xs = sorted({x for x1, _, x2, _ in rects for x in (x1, x2)})
ys = sorted({y for _, y1, _, y2 in rects for y in (y1, y2)})
assert xs == [0, 2, 3, 5] and ys == [0, 1, 2, 4]
cells = len(xs[:-1]) * len(ys[:-1])
assert cells == 3 * 3                           # tiny 3x3 grid, coordinates up to 5
# mark each cell against every rectangle: coverage is constant inside a cell
def area(rects):
    xs = sorted({x for x1, _, x2, _ in rects for x in (x1, x2)})
    ys = sorted({y for _, y1, _, y2 in rects for y in (y1, y2)})
    A = 0
    for xi in range(len(xs) - 1):
        for yi in range(len(ys) - 1):
            cx, cy = (xs[xi] + xs[xi + 1]) / 2, (ys[yi] + ys[yi + 1]) / 2
            if any(x1 <= cx < x2 and y1 <= cy < y2 for x1, y1, x2, y2 in rects):
                A += (xs[xi + 1] - xs[xi]) * (ys[yi + 1] - ys[yi])
    return A


assert area([(0, 0, 3, 2), (2, 1, 5, 4)]) == 3 * 2 + 3 * 3 - 1 * 1     # 6 + 9 - 1 overlap = 14
assert area([(0, 0, 1, 1)]) == 1
```

`area` is $O(n^3)$ for $n$ rectangles on a $2n$-cell grid — and with $n \le 200$ that beats any cleverer structure by simplicity (LC 850, @sec-coord-p5-area, where $10^9$ coordinates make the *cells* the only affordable world).

## Part B — Patterns

Each pattern below is one *shape of translation* between a huge universe and a small one. The two solved problems per pattern put that shape on a real contest problem.

**Where we are.** The five patterns climb one idea at a time on top of A1's rank map. Pattern 1 builds the map once and indexes a *structure* by rank — a Fenwick tree that finally gets used (@sec-coord-p1). Pattern 2 notices the queries are also data: sort *them* too and let one monotone pointer serve the whole batch, or let a growing edge pool serve a growing threshold (@sec-coord-p2). Pattern 3 flips time: deletions become insertions, and the state asked *after* each edit is read *before* its replayed twin (@sec-coord-p3). Pattern 4 moves the cut itself along the coordinate line, paying per event rather than per unit of space, and answers every coverage question from one walk (@sec-coord-p4). Pattern 5 generalises the rank map to two dimensions and beyond: compress both axes of a rectangle soup, or compress a whole pair-universe down to the $2k$ vertices that can possibly hold the answer (@sec-coord-p5). Pattern 1 is where the tooling lives; the other four are different answers to "what should the sorted order be?".

## P1. Compress, then index by rank {#sec-coord-p1}

**From a one-liner to a workhorse.** @sec-srt-a4 gave the map; here it earns its keep. The problems below take an object indexed by values that are too large or too sparse for a table — prefix sums up to $10^{10}$, array positions up to $10^9$ — and answer *rank questions* with A2's Fenwick tree over compressed coordinates.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Compress the *whole* universe that will ever be queried, once, before answering.** Gather every value that appears in input *or* in any query, `sorted(set(...))`, then index by rank. An offline gift: you know all queries in advance (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-a3's permission).
- **"How many earlier elements are smaller?" is a BIT prefix.** Scan left to right; `sum(rank(x) - 1)` asks, `add(rank(x), 1)` records. The same three lines count inversions, range-sum windows, and swapped-cell contributions (@sec-coord-a2, @sec-salgo-p2's merge twin).
- **Sparse positions are also compressible.** When *indices* reach $10^9$ but only $O(n)$ exist, the rank map points at positions instead of values — untouched runs in between are counted by arithmetic on coordinate differences, not iterated (@sec-coord-p1-invinfinite).
- **The oracle for everything above is the quadratic scan.** "How many earlier smaller" by nested loops runs in $O(n^2)$ on test-sized inputs; stress the $O(n \log n)$ structure against it (@sec-coord-a2's stress cell).
:::

{{< include ../problems/lc-0327-count-of-range-sum/problem.qmd >}}

[**From values to positions.** The previous problem compressed prefix *sums*; the next compresses array *indices* and shows the untouched integer runs between them are still answered by rank arithmetic.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-540e-infinite-inversions/problem.qmd >}}

## P2. Sort the queries, scan once {#sec-coord-p2}

**From one array to a batch of questions.** The queries are a second stream — sort them alongside the data and one pointer (or one growing structure) serves them all. Both problems below define a monotone *entry condition* — an element or edge becomes eligible when the threshold reaches it — and eligibility never unwinds.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Answer array + sorted index list = reordering with memory.** `order = sorted(range(q), key=lambda i: qs[i])`, sweep, write `ans[qi]`; print last (@sec-coord-a3).
- **A threshold sweep is a pointer when the pool only grows.** Elements sorted by value enter once; the running answer is read at each query's entrance point — CF 600B counts with one pointer, @sec-coord-p2-pathq merges with one DSU (@sec-coord-a4).
- **Bisect is the online twin of the sweep.** If the statement secretly forbids reordering, `bisect_right` on the sorted copy answers each query in $O(\log n)$ with zero bookkeeping (@sec-coord-a4, @sec-bst).
- **Price the precompute against the batch.** A $O(n \log n)$ sort plus $O(q)$ sweep beats $O(q)$ binary searches only when $q$ is large enough to matter; $q \le 100$ justifies the naive per-query scan (@sec-coord-a3's ledger).
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-600b-queries-about-less-or-equal-elements/problem.qmd >}}

[**From a pointer to a structure.** The previous problem's sweep state was one integer; when the entering data is a forest's edge pool, the growing state is a DSU and the answer is a component-pair count. Same sorted threshold, richer merge.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1213g-path-queries/problem.qmd >}}

## P3. Reverse the stream of operations {#sec-coord-p3}

**From deletions to insertions.** When every forward operation *breaks* something (removes an element, consumes a position), replay it backwards so every operation *builds* something. The state after the $k$-th forward deletion equals the state before the $k$-th backward insertion — one index of careful bookkeeping (A5's figure) away.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Write down both timelines.** Mark what each query asks: "after deletion $k$" answers correspond to "before re-adding the $k{+}1$-st" — build the answer array over $k = n \dots 0$ and read $1 \dots n$ (@sec-coord-a5).
- **Merges are reversible offline; splits are not online.** Blocks and components only *grow* under insertion, so a monotone aggregate (max block sum, component count) survives. The union of two live neighbours is an $O(\alpha)$ merge (@sec-lang-p4-tickets' DSU-on-positions twin).
- **"Find the value with the $k$-th smallest remaining order statistic" = BIT descent.** Once values are *removed as they are used*, the survivor set is a count-BIT over $1..n$; `kth` walks it in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-coord-a2, @sec-coord-p3-restore).
- **Sum-of-smaller witnesses pin the position.** When each record is "$\sum$ of earlier elements smaller than me", the *last* position reads its sum off the *entire unused pool* — the backward sweep turns prefix conditions into suffix availability (@sec-coord-p3-restore).
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-722c-destroying-array/problem.qmd >}}

[**From undoing damage to undoing greed.** Destroying a sequence backwards re-merges what deletion split; restoring a permutation backwards assigns positions from the end because the *earlier-than* relation dissolves into "whatever values are left" (@sec-coord-p3-restore).]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1208d-restore-permutation/problem.qmd >}}

## P4. Sweep the line and answer {#sec-coord-p4}

**From thresholds to coordinates.** A4's pointer walks *space* instead of rank: sort every event coordinate once, move the cut, and read the maintained state wherever a question lives. The two problems keep different state — a coverage counter, and a pair of count+sum BITs over compressed velocities — but both charge per event.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **$+1$ at $l$, $-1$ at $r+1$ turns closed intervals into half-open runs.** The stretch between consecutive event coordinates has constant coverage and costs one multiplication to charge (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-int-repr).
- **Group the deltas at one coordinate, then charge the run.** Order of work at a shared event point decides whether touching segments double-count their joint point (@sec-coord-a6's inner loop).
- **When the swept quantity feeds a *query into the maintained state*, replace the counter by a BIT over compressed keys.** "Sum over earlier points with $v_i \le v_j$" is A2's count+sum pair with $x$ as the weight (@sec-coord-p4-moving).
- **Sweeping is the cheapest online-allowed offline trick.** Sorting the *events* never sorts the *answers* — an endpoint sweep's output is a histogram, positionally independent (@sec-coord-a3's permission, observed or not).
:::

{{< include ../problems/cf-1000c-covered-points-count/problem.qmd >}}

[**From counting coverage to integrating cost.** The previous sweep maintained a counter over space; the next sweeps points by coordinate while maintaining a Fenwick pair over the *other* key, accumulating a quadratic total in $O(n \log n)$.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1311f-moving-points/problem.qmd >}}

## P5. Compress the space you touch {#sec-coord-p5}

**From one axis to all of them.** The last pattern drops the position axis entirely and asks: *what subset of this universe can possibly carry the answer?* For a rectangle union it is the $2n$ x-coordinates and $2n$ y-coordinates; for a k-th-smallest pair distance it is the $\le 2k$ endpoints of the $k$ lightest edges. Compress that set, work inside it, ignore the rest of the $10^9$-wide world.

::: {.callout-important title="Template"}
- **Compress each axis independently; the answer grid is the product of the two rank maps.** Cells between consecutive coordinates are *uniform* (constant coverage), so a cell is one test and one weight (A6's `area`).
- **Enumerate cells, not points; enumerate candidates, not the universe.** $n \le 200$ rectangles give $\le 400^2$ cells; $k \le 400$ light edges give $\le 800$ vertices. The constraint line in the statement is the compression's license (@sec-coord-p5-area, @sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
- **Prune by the $k$-th witness.** To find the $k$-th smallest among $O(n^2)$ pair distances, keep the $k$ smallest *edges* first: any qualifying pair-distance is $\le$ the $k$-th edge weight, and a vertex with no edge below it is irrelevant — delete it from the universe (@sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
- **The sweep and the grid are the same trade.** Sort-and-sweep pays per event ($O(n \log n)$ on one axis); the compressed grid pays per cell ($O(n^3)$ over both axes). When state per slice is complex, sweep; when the predicate is rectangular, grid (@sec-coord-a6 vs @sec-coord-p5-area).
:::

{{< include ../problems/lc-0850-rectangle-area-ii/problem.qmd >}}

[**From compressing coordinates to compressing a search space.** Rectangles taught the grid over sorted coordinates; the next problem keeps the same move — "the answer lives among $O(k)$ witnesses of an $O(n^2)$ universe" — with Dijkstra in place of the cell test.]{.flow-bridge}

{{< include ../problems/cf-1196f-k-th-path/problem.qmd >}}

**Looking back.** Every pattern here answered the same meta-question — *which order should the sorted thing be in?* P1 sorted the **values** to feed a structure; P2 sorted the **queries** to feed a pointer; P3 sorted **time** backwards to feed merges; P4 sorted **coordinates** to feed a maintained counter; P5 sorted whatever **slice of the universe** the answer is guaranteed to live in. The chain from Part A runs forward through them: A1's rank map is P1's opening line, A2's BIT is P1's engine and P4's, A3's permission and A4's sweep are P2's entire content, A5's replay is P3's, A6's events are P4's and P5's. Each pattern is one lesson promoted from a demo to a solved contest problem.

## Pattern map

| Signal in the statement | Pattern | Section |
|---|---|---|
| "Count / sum of values $\le v$ among *earlier* elements" | Rank map + BIT prefix | @sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-p1 |
| Values (or positions) up to $10^9$ but only $O(n)$ exist | Compress the universe, allocate by $n$ | @sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-p1-invinfinite |
| Prefix sums up to $10^{10}$; "range sums within $[lo, hi]$" | Compress prefix values, BIT by rank | @sec-coord-p1-rangesum |
| "$q$ queries, no updates" + one shared sorted order | Sort query indices, single pointer | @sec-coord-a3, @sec-coord-p2-lequal |
| "Edges of weight $\le q$; answer per $q$" | Threshold sweep with DSU merge counts | @sec-coord-p2-pathq |
| "After each deletion/undo, report …" | Replay backwards as insertions | @sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3-destroy |
| "Recover sequence from prefix-condition sums" | Right-to-left + order-statistics BIT | @sec-coord-p3-restore |
| Segment endpoints up to $10^{18}$; "exactly $k$ cover" | $+1/(r{+}1)\to-1$ events, sweep, charge runs | @sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered |
| Sum over pairs passing a *second* key condition | Sweep one axis, BIT the other (compressed) | @sec-coord-p4-moving |
| Rectangle union with $10^9$ coordinates | Compress both axes, mark uniform cells | @sec-coord-p5-area |
| $k$-th smallest over $O(n^2)$ pair distances | Keep $k$ lightest edges, compress to $2k$ vertices | @sec-coord-p5-kthpath |

## Pitfalls {#sec-coord-pit}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **Treating ranks as values.** $\mathit{gcd}$, residues, and differences need the original numbers; only order/equality questions survive compression (@sec-coord-a1's witness; contrast @sec-gcd-a3 where the value domain must stay raw).
- **Compressing only the input, not the queries.** A BIT built over ranks of `a` cannot answer "how many $\le t$" when $t$ is a *query* value absent from `a` — collect the union of both streams before `sorted(set(...))` (@sec-coord-a1; `bisect` variants dodge it automatically).
- **`bisect_left` where `bisect_right` was needed.** "Strictly less" is `bisect_left`; "less or equal" is `bisect_right`. One index off means every equal-valued element miscounted (@sec-coord-a4, CF 600B asks $\le$).
- **Printing while sweeping an offline batch.** Answers computed in sorted-query order must land in `ans[qi]`; printing in sweep order scrambles the output and looks like a wrong algorithm (@sec-coord-a3's discipline).
- **Reordering queries that feed later queries.** If query $i{+}1$'s input depends on answer $i$ (or updates interleave), the batch is online; a sorted sweep silently uses future information (@sec-coord-a3).
- **Off-by-one in the backward replay.** "After deletion $k$" corresponds to the state *after* re-adding deletions $n \dots k{+}1$, not $k$. Write the correspondence table once (A5's `ans[k] = best` placement) and code it literally.
- **Charging the run *after* applying deltas at a shared coordinate.** Two segments touching at $x$ must both be active while charging the stretch ending at $x$ — apply deltas only after `cnt[cur] += x - prev` (@sec-coord-a6's grouping loop).
- **Forgetting the $+1$ in $r + 1$ on a $10^{18}$ endpoint.** The value itself fits a signed 64-bit, but in C++ an `int` or a careless `long long` mix in `r + 1` overflows near $10^{18}$ and the sweep's last run vanishes (@sec-lang-costs, @sec-arr-size-trap).
- **Counting ordered pairs where unordered are wanted.** Pair universes are $\binom{n}{2}$: a $k$-th-smallest candidate list built from Dijkstra rows includes $(u,u)$ (distance $0$) and both $(u,v),(v,u)$ — dedupe or count half (@sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
- **A 32-bit accumulator over the sweep's histogram.** Count of points $\times$ coordinate span reaches $10^{18}$s in coverage and pair-sum problems; every Part B running total is `long long` (@sec-arr-size-trap).
:::

## Exercises

**1. [E] Compress `[10**9, -10**9, 7, 7, 3]` by hand with `rank_map`. What is the sum of the ranks of the two `7`s, and does that sum mean anything in the original values?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Sorted distinct: $[-10^9, 3, 7, 10^9]$, so $\mathit{rank}(-10^9)=1$, $\mathit{rank}(3)=2$, $\mathit{rank}(7)=3$ (both copies), $\mathit{rank}(10^9)=4$. The two 7s contribute $3+3=6$; in original values $7+7=14 \ne 6$. Rank sums are meaningless unless the *same* multiset question is posed entirely in ranks (@sec-coord-a1).
:::

**2. [E] After `add(3, 5)`, `add(5, 2)`, `add(8, 1)` on a length-8 BIT, which tree cells changed and why does `sum(7) = t[7] + t[6] + t[4]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
`add(3, 5)` walks $3 \to 4 \to 8$; `add(5, 2)` walks $5 \to 6 \to 8$; `add(8, 1)` touches $8$ only. So $t[3]=5$, $t[4]=5$, $t[5]=2$, $t[6]=2$, $t[8]=8$. `sum(7)` strips lowest bits $7 \to 6 \to 4 \to 0$: the ranges $[7,7] + [5,6] + [1,4]$ tile $[1,7]$ exactly, giving $0 + 2 + 5 = 7$ (@sec-coord-a2's figure).
:::

**3. [E] With the sweep of @sec-coord-a6, how many integer points get coverage exactly 1, 2, 3 for segments `[0,3], [1,2], [2,5]`?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$0{:}1, 1{:}2, 2{:}3, 3{:}1, 4{:}1, 5{:}1$ → cnt1 $=4$ (points $0,3,4,5$), cnt2 $=1$ (point $1$), cnt3 $=1$ (point $2$) — asserted by the lesson's own cell (@sec-coord-a6).
:::

**4. [E] A stream deletes positions in order `[2, 1]` from `a = [4, 1]`. List the forward questions and the matching backward states.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Forward: after deleting pos 2 → `[4, x]`, best $=4$; after deleting pos 1 → `[x, x]$, best $=0$. Backward: start empty; re-add pos 1 → `{4}` (this is the state *after* the first forward deletion — ans[1] $=4$); re-add pos 2 → `{4,1}` (state before any deletion). The answer after the last forward deletion is read before the first backward insert (@sec-coord-a5).
:::

**5. [M] Why can't CF 1294D (@sec-mex-p2-mex-max) compress its array values before bucketing by modulus?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Its query adds $y \equiv n \pmod x$ — a statement about raw residues. Compression preserves $\le$ and $=$, not $\bmod$; two values with the same rank pattern can have different residues, and the counter would bucket wrong (@sec-coord-a1, Pitfall 1).
:::

**6. [M] Your $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ array is static; queries ask "how many elements in $[lo, hi]$" as $t$ ranges over $10^9$. Give the offline and online answers and their costs, and say which needs `sorted(set())` over *two* streams.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Online: sort `a` once, `bisect_right(hi) - bisect_left(lo)` per query, $O(\log n)$ each, no compression at all. Offline threshold form (A4): sort queries by `hi`, sweep once. The *compression* two-stream rule applies when the structure is a BIT over ranks — there both input values and query bounds must exist in the rank space (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-a4).
:::

**7. [M] Give the "first missing rank" $O(\log n)$ method with a count-BIT over `present` (the MEX-under-deletions ask of @sec-mex-pit).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Store `present[r]` as $+1$ entries in a BIT; $\operatorname{MEX}$ is the smallest $r$ with $\mathit{sum}(r) < r$ — i.e. the first rank whose prefix is short. Binary descent on the BIT finds $\mathit{kth}(k)$ = first prefix reaching $k$; walking $k$ to its own value gives the first hole in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-coord-a2).
:::

**8. [M] CF 722C asked max block *sum*. Does the backward trick still work for max block *product*?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Not with a single monotone aggregate: products don't merge with `max` — a negative-heavy block's product can lose to both parts', and zeros destroy ranges. Backward replay needs *some* easy merge rule; here keep the whole multiset per component and track best via sorted ends, or answer differently (@sec-coord-a5).
:::

**9. [M] For the $n \le 2000$ all-subarrays framing of @sec-mex-p5-special, would a compressed-positions BIT make it $O(n \log n)$? Which line of the statement stops you?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
No. The predicate is "$a_i$ **equals** some subarray sum" — an arithmetic match against raw values, and all $O(n^2)$ sums genuinely exist; compressing the sum values still requires *enumerating* them. The $n \le 2000$ line is the problem admitting $O(n^2)$ (@sec-mex-p5-special, @sec-coord-a1's destroy-list).
:::

**10. [M] Run the LC 327 solution by hand on `nums = [-2, 5, -1]`, `lower = -2`, `upper = 2`. Which prefix sums enter the BIT and when?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Prefixes $P = [0, -2, 3, 2]$; compressed ranks $-2{:}1, 0{:}2, 2{:}3, 3{:}4$. Insert $P_0$, then for each $j$ count inserted prefix values inside $[P_j - 2,\; P_j + 2]$ before inserting $P_j$. $j=1$ ($P=-2$): window $[-4, 0]$ sees $\{0\}$ → 1. $j=2$ ($P=3$): window $[1, 5]$ sees $\{0, -2\}$ → 0. $j=3$ ($P=2$): window $[0, 4]$ sees $\{0, -2, 3\}$ → 2 (the 0 and the 3). Total $1 + 0 + 2 = 3$, matching the subarrays $[-2]$, $[-1]$, $[-2,5,-1]$ (@sec-coord-p1-rangesum).
:::

**11. [M] A single `swap(a, b)` on the identity sequence $1, 2, \ldots$ ($a < b$) creates how many inversions? Prove it.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p_a = b$, $p_b = a$: the pair $(a, b)$ inverts; each untouched $q \in (a, b)$ inverts with *both* moved cells — $(a, q)$ because $b > q$, and $(q, b)$ because $q > a$ — giving $2(b - a - 1) + 1$ total. Multi-swap compositions are where touched cells can also invert each other, which is why @sec-coord-p1-invinfinite counts touched-vs-touched pairs separately with a BIT, stress-tested against a full simulation.
:::

**12. [H] Prove: if a vertex $u$ is not an endpoint of any of the $k$ lightest edges of a graph, its shortest distance to *any* vertex is $\ge w_k$ (the weight of the $k$-th lightest edge).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every edge incident to $u$ has weight $\ge w_k$ (else $u$ would end a lighter edge, among the $k$ lightest... careful with ties: use "$>$ the kept set's max" bookkeeping as the problem does). Any $u$-anchored path starts with such an edge; lengths are positive, so distance $\ge w_k$. And the $\le k$ kept edges already offer pairs at distances $\le w_k$ — so the $k$-th smallest pair-distance is realised between kept vertices (@sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
:::

**13. [H] Design: a hotel books $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ stays $(\mathit{start}, \mathit{end})$ on a $10^9$-day year. Report, for each $k = 0 \dots n$, how many days have exactly $k$ bookings. State the data you sort and the loop invariant of the walk.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Events $(\mathit{start}, +1)$, $(\mathit{end} + 1, -1)$; sort; invariant "between consecutive event coordinates, coverage $=$ cur, length charged". Invariant + grouping at shared coordinates is exactly @sec-coord-a6's `coverage_counts`; degenerate one-day stays become $+1/-1$ at $(d, d{+}1)$.
:::

**14. [M] Estimate memory: a `present` table for positions up to $10^9$ versus a rank map over $2 \cdot 10^5$ touched positions (Python ints are 28 bytes; C++ `long long` 8). Why does Python's version still need care?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$10^9$ C++ cells $\approx 8$ GB, impossible; Python list would be worse ($\approx 8$ GB of pointers). Compressed: dict/list over $4 \cdot 10^5$ cells — tens of MB in Python. Care line: touched *distinct* count ($\le 2n$), not operation count, sizes the table (@sec-coord-p1-invinfinite, @sec-arr-cost).
:::

**15. [M] In @sec-coord-p3-restore, explain why processing positions right-to-left converts "smaller *earlier* elements" into "any unused smaller value". Which direction makes `s_n` readable in one lookup?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
At position $i$ every value not yet consumed lives at positions $\le i$; if $p_i = v$ then the unused pool minus $v$ all sits at positions $< i$, so $s_i$ is exactly the sum of unused values $< v$ — one prefix-sum read on the BIT over values (right-to-left direction). For $i = n$ the pool is all of $1..n$: $s_n$ *is* the prefix-sum target, read off by `kth`-descent in $O(\log n)$ (@sec-coord-p3-restore, @sec-coord-a2).
:::

**16. [H] Your event sweep produced answers at coordinates; the problem asks about *integer* points, and your $-1$ events use $r + 1$. Give two distinct bugs that arise when the endpoints were instead real numbers (a union-length question, LC 850-style).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(1) $r + 1$ is wrong for reals — the half-open twin is exactly $r$; the $+1$ exists only because integer points are discrete (a gap of one between $r$ and $r+1$). (2) "Points" become "length", so run-charges multiply by coordinate differences instead of counting units, and shared coordinates need delta-sums before/after charging per the *same* grouping rule (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered).
:::

## Interview questions

**1. What is coordinate compression, and what two guarantees does the rank map keep?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A translation of arbitrary comparable values to dense indices $1 \ldots |\text{distinct}|$ via `sorted(set(a))` + dict (or bisect). It keeps exactly: (i) $x < y \iff \mathit{rank}(x) < \mathit{rank}(y)$; (ii) $x = y \iff \mathit{rank}(x) = \mathit{rank}(y)$. It drops arithmetic — gaps, sums, mod — hence it's valid only when the algorithm's comparisons never see raw values (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-srt-a4).
:::

**2. Count "how many earlier elements are smaller than me" for every position. Give two $O(n \log n)$ answers and their trade-offs.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Merge-sort counting across the merge (@sec-salgo-p2 — LC 315's home method) and BIT over compressed ranks (@sec-coord-a2). The divide version is static, batch, recursion-heavy; the BIT version handles *interleaved* "how many smaller seen so far" online and generalises to sums (`range_sum`) and order statistics (`kth`).
:::

**3. Why can't a hash-map prefix count solve "number of subarrays with sum in $[lo, hi]$" when values can be negative, and what does?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The hash form answers exact-key equality $P_j - P_i = s$; a *range* $[lo, hi]$ needs order statistics — "count earlier $P_i \in [P_j - hi, P_j - lo]$" — which is a BIT over compressed prefix values ($O(\log n)$ per step) or merge-count; that's LC 327, the promise @sec-pref-hash left open (@sec-coord-p1-rangesum).
:::

**4. You're given a static array and $10^5$ queries "how many elements $\le t$". Then a variant with point updates interleaved. Solve both.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Static: sort once; either offline sweep ($O(n\log n + q)$, @sec-coord-a3) or `bisect_right` per query ($O(\log n)$ each, online). With interleaved updates: neither works — a value-indexed structure is mandatory: BIT over compressed positions/values (the Fenwick "later volume" promise; LC 307 is its textbook drill) (@sec-coord-a2).
:::

**5. A stream deletes elements from an array; after each deletion report the largest contiguous-block sum. Sketch the solution and state why forward is hopeless.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Reverse time: replay deletions as insertions; an inserted cell activates, unions with live neighbours, component sums grow monotonically; track the running best. Forward is hopeless because *splitting* a block needs re-searching inside it; merging is $O(\alpha)$ (@sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3-destroy).
:::

**6. Explain the Fenwick `kth` descent: why is walking the tree by powers of two a binary search?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
From $i = 0$, try $j = i + 2^b$ downward in bits: if $t[j] < k$, then all of $j$'s covered range lies inside the answer's prefix, so commit $i = j$, $k -= t[j]$. It mirrors finding the largest prefix with sum $< k_{\text{target}}$ by binary representation instead of midpoints; each step halves the remaining candidates. Costs $O(\log n)$ and requires non-negative entries (@sec-coord-a2).
:::

**7. Segments over $[0, 10^{18}]$, count integer points covered exactly $k$ times, for every $k$. Give the algorithm and the two implementation traps.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Events $(l, +1), (r+1, -1)$, sort, sweep; charge `cur` coverage to stretches `x - prev` between grouped events. Traps: (1) apply deltas at a shared coordinate *after* charging; (2) $r + 1$ overflows 32-bit and needs care at $10^{18}$ boundaries (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered).
:::

**8. Sum the union area of $n \le 200$ axis-aligned rectangles with integer coordinates up to $10^9$ (LC 850). Two approaches and their complexities.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Compress both axes: unique x- and y-coordinates ($\le 2n$ each), mark the $\le 4n^2$ uniform cells against each rectangle — $O(n^3)$, trivially correct (mod $10^9+7$ at the end). Sweep one axis with an interval-coverage counter on the other — $O(n^2 \log n)$ — heavier to code. At $n = 200$ the cubic cell loop is the intended path (@sec-coord-p5-area, @sec-coord-a6).
:::

**9. Given a permutation encoded by $s_i$ = "sum of earlier elements smaller than $p_i$", restore it. Why process right-to-left and what structure?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Right-to-left, every not-yet-used value sits at earlier positions, so $s_i$ = sum of unused values $< p_i$: a prefix-sum lookup over a live-values BIT, then *find the largest prefix whose sum is $\le s_i$* and take the next survivor — `kth`-style descent, $O(\log n)$ per position, $O(n \log n)$ total, with the sum-BIT alongside the count-BIT to remove (@sec-coord-p3-restore).
:::

**10. Points on a line with velocities; sum of minimum pair distances. Reduce to a sweep + compressed BIT in one minute.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Two points meet iff the left one's velocity is greater; otherwise $\min$ distance $=$ initial gap. Sort by coordinate; sweep left-to-right; at $j$ the contributing earlier points are those with $v_i \le v_j$ — count and coordinate-sum among them via two BITs over compressed velocities, answer $+ = x_j \cdot \mathit{cnt} - \mathit{sum}$ (@sec-coord-p4-moving).
:::

**11. When must you *refuse* to sort the queries? Two statement features to spot.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(1) Updates interleaved with queries (the data moves while you plan to batch-read it). (2) Adaptive queries — the statement says the next query depends on your previous answer (interactive or XOR-encrypted input like several CF problems). Both make any "sort the queries" order illegal; the online structures (bisect on rebuilt pieces, BIT, segment tree) are the fallback (@sec-coord-a3).
:::

**12. $n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ vertices, $m \le 2 \cdot 10^5$ edges, $k \le 400$; find the $k$-th smallest pairwise shortest distance. What is the compression argument?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Keep the $k$ lightest edges; call their endpoints relevant ($\le 2k$). Any pair with both vertices irrelevant has distance $\ge w_k$, while the kept edges alone already witness $\ge k$ pairs at distance $\le w_k$ — so the answer sits between relevant vertices. Run Dijkstra from each relevant vertex (early exit when all relevant settled), collect relevant-relevant distances, take the $k$-th smallest of deduped unordered pairs (@sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
:::

**13. "Compress the tree" (virtual trees) is a phrase you'll meet in the trees volume. In one paragraph: what does the same habit look like there?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
On a tree, a batch of $k$ *marked* vertices induces a minimal Steiner-like subtree; the "space you touch" is the union of root-paths through LCAs, so compress $n$ tree vertices to the $O(k)$ marked ones + their $O(k)$ LCAs, sorted by Euler order. Identical logic: bound the answer's witnesses, keep only those coordinates, rebuild adjacency by parent jumps (ch. 185 "virtual trees" in the roadmap; cf. @sec-coord-p5-kthpath's endpoint-pool argument).
:::

## Summary

::: {.callout-important title="Templates to remember"}
- **The rank map.** `rank = {v: i + 1 for i, v in enumerate(sorted(set(UNIV)))}` where `UNIV` includes *every value the queries will ask*. Order/equality only; arithmetic is destroyed (@sec-coord-a1).
- **The compressed BIT.** `add(rank, delta)`, `sum(rank)` prefix, `kth(k)` descent — three walks of the `i & -i` / `i -= i & -i` ladder; $O(\log n)$ each over $n$ dense ranks (@sec-coord-a2).
- **The offline ledger.** Sort query indices, sweep data with one monotone pointer, write `ans[qi]`, print at the end. Legal iff no interleaved updates and no adaptive queries (@sec-coord-a3, @sec-coord-a4).
- **The backward replay.** Answers after $k$ forward deletions = state before the $(n-k)$-th backward insertion. Merge-only structures (block sums, DSU, nearest-survivor pointers) serve this perfectly (@sec-coord-a5).
- **The event sweep.** $+1$ at $l$, $-1$ at $r+1$; sort; charge `cur × (x - prev)` between coordinates, group deltas at shared $x$. $O(n \log n)$ regardless of universe width (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4).
- **Touch-universe compression.** Collect the $O(k)$ or $O(n)$ coordinates/vertices/edges the answer provably lives among; compress; enumerate inside it. Rectangles: both axes. $k$-th path: the $2k$ endpoints of the $k$ lightest edges (@sec-coord-p5).
:::

- The whole chapter is one sentence: *you may sort anything* — values (P1), queries (P2), time (P3), space (P4), or the answer's candidate set (P5) — and *you may translate values to ranks* whenever only comparisons are read after the translation (@sec-coord-a1, @sec-coord-why).
- Compression and the BIT are a package: the map makes indices dense, the tree makes prefix questions logarithmic. Earlier chapters promised exactly this pairing (@sec-cnt-a3, @sec-salgo-p2, @sec-mex-pit's exercise); @sec-coord-a2 cashed it.
- Offline reordering has a hard boundary: interleaved updates and adaptive queries. Spotting it is a statement-reading skill, not a coding one — when in doubt, the `bisect`/online structures cost you only a $\log n$ (@sec-coord-a3, @sec-coord-a4).
- Deletions are insertions in a mirror: the backward replay converts split-hard questions into merge-easy ones, and the correspondence table ("after $k$ forward = before re-adding the $(k{+}1)$-st") is the only place bugs survive — write it down once (@sec-coord-a5, @sec-coord-p3).
- Sweeps charge per event, never per unit of space: $10^{18}$-wide coordinates shrink to $4n$ event points; the $r+1$ convention and grouped deltas are the two integer-grit details (@sec-coord-a6, @sec-coord-p4-covered).
- The pair universe $O(n^2)$ and the grid universe $(10^9)^2$ share the escape: prove the answer sits among $O(k)$ or $O(n)$ witnesses, compress to them, brute force *inside* the compressed world (@sec-coord-p5-area, @sec-coord-p5-kthpath).
- 64-bit vigilance is the tax of every large universe: coverage spans, pair sums, and prefix targets all exceed $2^{31}$ in the mid; the rank map shrinks indices but not magnitudes (@sec-arr-size-trap, @sec-lang-costs).

## Further reading

- [CP-Algorithms — Fenwick Tree](https://cp-algorithms.com/data_structures/fenwick.html) — the structure of @sec-coord-a2 with range-update variants and the `kth` descent written three ways.
- [Wikipedia — Fenwick tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fenwick_tree) — the `lowbit` derivation and history (it predates its name's contest fame).
- [Wikipedia — Sweep line algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweep_line_algorithm) — the geometric framing of @sec-coord-a6; Bentley–Ottmann is what the *general* segment-intersection sweep pays per event.
- [USACO Guide — Binary Indexed Trees](https://usaco.guide/plat/BIT) — problem sets ranked between @sec-coord-a2 and @sec-coord-p1; good for drilling the count+sum double-BIT.
- [CPH — Chapter 9 (Advanced Data Structures)](https://cses.fi/book/book.pdf) — the book's own BIT/segment-tree chapter; the trees-volume preview @sec-coord-a2 promised.
- [Wikipedia — Disjoint-set data structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disjoint-set_data_structure) — the merge engine behind @sec-coord-a5's replay and @sec-coord-p2-pathq; union-by-size bounds it at $O(\alpha(n))$.
- [Codeforces EDU — Data Structures](https://codeforces.com/edu/course/2) — interactive lessons for the ordered-structure family that replaces these offline tricks when updates interleave (@sec-coord-a3's boundary).
